title: Timbuktu's manuscripts
hookLine: a city of scholars, with the Sankore mosque and its manuscripts kept in family libraries

lines: A REAL TOWN ON THE NIGER.
cards: In English, "from here to Timbuktu" means the end of the earth, a place so far away it might as well be invented. But Timbuktu is real. It sits near the bend of the Niger, at the edge of the desert.
In its mud-brick houses, families kept wooden chests and cupboards full of handwritten books, some pages brittle and brown, with notes squeezed into the margins.
A traveler known as Leo Africanus passed through and noticed something strange about the market: books were among the most valuable things for sale. Today: Timbuktu's manuscripts.

teach.h: BY THE PEN AND WHAT THEY WRITE.
teach.b: One surah of the Qur'an, revealed to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, is named al-Qalam, the Pen, and it opens with an oath. In Pickthall's translation: "Nun. By the pen and that which they write (therein)."

teach.h: BOOKS WORTH MORE THAN OTHER GOODS.
teach.b: Leo Africanus wrote that the town had many judges, teachers and learned men, paid by the king, and that handwritten books brought from North Africa sold there for more than any other merchandise.

Scholars gathered at mosques like Sankore, and students sat with teachers one book at a time, often copying the book for themselves as they studied it. What's in the manuscripts? Copies of the Qur'an, yes.

But also law, grammar, the life of the Prophet, Sufi poetry, astronomy for setting prayer times, medicine, letters between scholars, records of sales and debts and marriages. A whole town's mind, written down.
The chronicler al-Sa'di remembers the scholar Ahmad Baba, who was carried away from Timbuktu into exile after Moroccan forces took the city. Tradition says he mourned the books he lost.
Families kept the rest, generation after generation, and tradition says some were hidden in walls or buried in the sand.
And in recent years, when armed men held the town, librarians and families carried manuscripts away to safety in trunks. Gold passed through Timbuktu. The pages stayed.

how: Families and libraries in Timbuktu still keep manuscripts, and scholars and conservators work to preserve, catalog and photograph them so they can be read.

games.q: armed men have taken your town, and your family's chest of old manuscripts is in the house. what do you do?
o: leave them and hope for the best.
carry them away to safety, hidden in trunks.
sell them while you still can.
games.why: in our own time, librarians and families carried manuscripts out of Timbuktu in trunks, as families before them had hidden them in walls and sand.

practice: Go back over what the chests held: law, grammar, the life of the Prophet, poetry, the stars, medicine, letters, records of debts and marriages, and let one of them catch your interest.

Suppose a family in Timbuktu lifted the lid and let you read a single page on it: what would you hope to find out? If you pray, give thanks for the scholars who wrote and the families who kept; if not, simply hold the question.

wordCard.voice: Timbuktu's manuscripts. The handwritten books of a West African city of scholars, on law, faith, stars and medicine, kept by families and carried to safety. Today's word.
